numbers.headline: Of Israeli adults surveyed twice, 138 fit the pattern the authors call 'recovery' from a porn or sex problem; 42 fit 'chronic'.
numbers.mirror: You've tried to stop before and think you're stuck with this for good.
numbers.counted: adults whose questionnaire answers showed a probable porn or sex problem

basis.design: community cohort surveyed four times; people were sorted into groups by a statistical model (latent profile analysis) using the 2018 and 2022 surveys
basis.who: Jewish adults in Israel aged 18 to 70, from a community sample
basis.n: 180 in the two groups whose names say the problem was there in 2018: 138 'recovery' and 42 'chronic' (of 1,182 sorted into four groups)
basis.measured: Self-report questionnaires for probable compulsive sexual behaviour disorder and problem porn use at both surveys. 'Recovery' and 'chronic' are the authors' names for the groups.

numbers.caveat: Questionnaire scores, not a doctor's diagnosis, and porn and sex problems are counted together. 'Recovery' is the authors' name for a group a model drew; it does not show that each of the 138 dropped below a problem line. It says nothing about how they changed or whether it lasted after 2022.
numbers.weak: How the model drew the 'recovery' group is unchecked, so it may not mean each person got free; how many were men is unknown; porn and sex problems are mixed.

ref.cite: Efrati Y, Shmulewitz D, Skvirsky V, Vider M, Kor A, Lev-Ran S, Mikulincer M (2026). Longitudinal study of probable compulsive sexual behavior disorder and problematic pornography use profiles: their prospective impact on psychopathology during wartime. Addictive Behaviors, article 108589.

problems: The headline is more hopeful than the source. The abstract gives the group sizes and the authors' names for them ('recovery' n = 138, 'chronic' n = 42, of 1,182) and nothing more. It does not say what 'recovery' means in scores, or that the 138 'no longer had it' in 2022. Latent profile groups are drawn from average score patterns, so a 'recovery' member may have scored lower without dropping below a problem line. The full text is CC-BY (hybrid open access), but ScienceDirect served a captcha to every route tried. The Elsevier text-mining API returned metadata only. Until someone reads the methods, the card must use the authors' label, not 'no longer had it'.

basis.n says the 180 'scored as having a probable problem at the first survey'. The abstract does not say this. It is inferred from the group names. Others in 'no disorder' could also have scored above a cut-off in 2018.
basis.who and weak say 'men and women'. The abstract says only 'community sample of Jewish population in Israel, aged 18-70' and gives no sex split. This is probably true but unchecked.
basis.design says 'surveyed twice'. The cohort was surveyed four times (2018, 2022, then two waves during the war, 'Using T3 and T4'). The profiles come from the first two.
Rule 9 build lint: weak contains 'fetched' ('Only the abstract could be fetched'), which is in the banned research-note list for reader text.

Kind hope-free-now asks for people 'already free, counted, not projected'. A model-drawn 'recovery' class is not a head count of people below a problem line. This is a weak hero; the caveat and weak lines must say so.

Holds: the quote is word for word in the abstract (17 words). 1,182 = 952+138+50+42. Surveys 2018 and 2022 hold, and so does the April 2026 issue (online 2025). The figures match. Severity 'disorder' (probable CSBD/PPU by self-report screen) is plausible but cut-offs are unchecked. The mirror is 13 words, in the second person, and not a screening line. The headline is 22 words with 2 digit figures ('four years later' adds a third number in words).
check1.applied: Applied on 2026-11-05: the reviewer's corrections word for word.
applierNotes: Open doubt, no field change: the reviewer's headline says 'surveyed twice' and its basis.design says 'surveyed four times'. Both hold: the groups come from the two pre-war surveys (2018 and 2022) of four. A re-checker may prefer 'surveyed in 2018 and 2022' in the headline.
Re-fetched the Europe PMC record on 2026-11-05: still abstract only (no PMC copy); the quote and the group sizes match it word for word.

numbers.headline: Of men who wanted help for their porn use, 4 in 10 had already tried to quit four or more times.
numbers.mirror: You've tried to quit four times and think a fifth is pointless.
numbers.counted: men who said they wanted help for their porn use

basis.who: men who watch porn, found mostly through Craigslist ads; average age 33 among those who wanted help
basis.n: 186 men who wanted help for their porn use (of 1,298 surveyed)
basis.where: USA, Canada and other English-speaking countries
basis.measured: Past tries to quit porn completely and to cut back: none, 1 to 3, or 4 or more. Among men who did not want help, 6% had tried to quit four or more times.

numbers.caveat: One survey at one moment, so it cannot say whether these men got free later or how many tries quitting usually takes. Volunteers who answered an ad.
numbers.weak: It counts tries so far by men still struggling, not the tries it took men who got free; no porn study counts those.

ref.cite: Kraus SW, Martino S, Potenza MN (2016). Clinical characteristics of men interested in seeking treatment for use of pornography. Journal of Behavioral Addictions 5:169-178.
ref.quote: Quit attempts with porn 0 attempts (“never”) 25.3 75.0 251.05 <0.001 1-to-3 past attempts 34.4 19.2 4+ past attempts 40.3 5.8

problems: Figure holds: Table 1, quit attempts with porn, 4+ past attempts = 40.3% of treatment-interested men vs 5.8% of the others (the 6% in 'measured' is right).

n holds: Table 1 column 'Yes (n = 186)'; Results: 'Out of the 1,298 individuals surveyed, 14.3% (n = 186) reported a current interest in seeking treatment'. Average age of that group 32.8, so 'average age 33' is right.

Group: 'self-hooked' is the closest tag. These men said they were interested in treatment; they were not in treatment (only 21.5% had ever sought it). 71% of them scored at or above the HBI cut-off for possible hypersexual disorder, so 'wanted help for their porn use' is fair.

Where/when/design hold: online survey, June-July 2013, 88% recruited through Craigslist; about 81% USA, 8% Canada, 11% other English-speaking countries. Journal of Behavioral Addictions 5(2):169-178, PMID 27348557.

Quote is word for word but it is a Table 1 row read across its cells (21 words), not a sentence. No prose sentence in the paper gives the 40.3%, so it stays; the card should not present it as a sentence the authors wrote.
Rules hold: headline 21 words, 2 figures ('4 in 10', 'four or more'); mirror 12 words, second person, not a screening line; no other addiction, no cheering, not a projection.

numbers.headline: Of 104 men keeping an online journal while quitting porn, 55 wrote about slipping at least once.
numbers.mirror: You broke your streak and think the whole attempt was wasted.
numbers.counted: men on a quit-porn forum, most calling themselves addicted

basis.design: study of online quitting journals, with no comparison group
basis.who: men aged 18 to 63 on the Reboot Nation forum; 80 of the 104 called themselves addicted to porn
basis.measured: Slips the men wrote about, and how long each journal's attempt ran. Only journals covering 7 days to 12 months were picked. At least 86.5% were also trying to stop masturbating.

numbers.caveat: Many men just stopped writing, so nobody knows how their attempts ended, and the study does not say when in an attempt the slips came. Half the journals covered 36.5 days or less. Men who journal in public may differ from men who quit quietly.
numbers.weak: A forum sample of 104 men, read from their own posts, with no record of when the slips happened.

ref.cite: Fernandez DP, Kuss DJ, Griffiths MD (2021). The pornography “rebooting” experience: a qualitative analysis of abstinence journals on an online pornography abstinence forum. Archives of Sexual Behavior 50:711-728.
ref.quote: More than half of the sample (n = 55) reported at least one lapse during their abstinence attempt.

problems: No problem found. The quote is word for word: 'More than half of the sample (n = 55) reported at least one lapse during their abstinence attempt.' (17 words). N = 104 men, age range 18 to 63. 80 reported being addicted to pornography. Journals were picked from 2016 to 2018, and each had to last at least seven days but no longer than 12 months. At least 86.5% also meant to stop masturbating. The median inferred attempt was 36.5 days. The source supports the caveat that members may have stopped posting. The cite (Arch Sex Behav 50:711-728, 2021) holds.

Minor, no change needed: the paper does not itself call Reboot Nation 'English-language'. The journals it quotes are in English. Severity 'self-hooked' fits (77% said they were addicted; the 55 are counted from all 104), and the kind how-slips allows it. The headline is 17 words with 2 figures, and the mirror is 11 words in the second person.

numbers.headline: In a small trial, men in ACT talk therapy cut porn viewing 93% on average, against 21% on a waiting list.
numbers.mirror: You've tried willpower alone and want a method that works.
numbers.counted: men in a therapy trial for problem porn use

basis.design: randomised trial (ACT therapy vs waiting list)
basis.who: adult men with problematic internet porn use; all but one were Latter-day Saints
basis.n: 28 men, split between therapy and a waiting list
basis.measured: Self-reported porn viewing before and after 12 one-to-one sessions of acceptance and commitment therapy (ACT).

numbers.caveat: It does not show that ACT beats other therapy: there was no comparison therapy. The 93% was measured at the end of therapy. Once the waiting-list men had therapy too, viewing across all 26 men was down 86% three months later, and 35% had stopped completely.
numbers.weak: Only 28 men, almost all from one church, and viewing was self-reported.

ref.cite: Crosby JM, Twohig MP (2016). Acceptance and commitment therapy for problematic internet pornography use: a randomized trial. Behavior Therapy 47:355-366.
ref.quote: significant between-condition reductions in pornography viewing compared to the waitlist condition (93% reduction ACT vs. 21% waitlist)

problems: Figure, quote, n and group hold against the abstract: 28 adult males, all but 1 Latter-day Saints, 12-session individual ACT protocol vs waitlist, '93% reduction ACT vs. 21% waitlist'. Quote is word for word (16 words). 'treatment' tag fits a therapy trial.

Headline reads as if each man cut viewing 93%. The 93% is the ACT group's reduction at the end of therapy (post-treatment), a group figure. Three months later the drop across all 26 men was 86% and only 35% had stopped completely, so the headline should say 'on average' and the caveat should say when the 93% was measured.

Only the abstract is open (full text paywalled; Semantic Scholar lists it CLOSED). The split of the 28 between arms and the trial dates could not be checked. 'USA' is supported only by the authors' Utah State University affiliation.
Rules otherwise hold: mirror 10 words, second person, not a screening line; no other addiction, no cheering, not a projection.
check1.applied: Applied on 2026-11-05: the reviewer's corrections word for word.
applierNotes: Spot check, abstract re-fetched 2026-11-05: 'When combining all participants (N=26), a 92% reduction was seen at posttreatment and an 86% reduction at 3-month follow-up' and '35% of participants showed complete cessation' hold.

numbers.headline: Porn users, most not hooked, asked to stop for 7 days felt no more withdrawal or craving than those who kept watching.
numbers.mirror: You fear the first week off will be unbearable.
numbers.counted: regular porn users, most not hooked

basis.who: psychology undergraduates who watched porn 3 or more times a week; 64% women, average age 21
basis.n: 176: 86 asked to stop for 7 days, 90 who kept watching
basis.measured: Each night for 7 days: craving, good and bad mood, and withdrawal symptoms, compared between the two groups after allowing for starting scores.

numbers.caveat: Most were not hooked: 85% scored below the problem cut-off, 9 in 10 had no wish to quit, and 45% of the stop group watched anyway. In an extra check, daily users with the highest problem scores who stopped felt more craving, so this does not show that hooked daily users get no withdrawal. Nothing was measured after day 7.
numbers.weak: Students, mostly women and mostly not hooked, followed for one week only.

ref.cite: Fernandez DP, Kuss DJ, Justice LV, Fernandez EF, Griffiths MD (2023). Effects of a 7-day pornography abstinence period on withdrawal-related symptoms in regular pornography users: a randomized controlled study. Archives of Sexual Behavior 52:1819-1840.
ref.quote: generally does not experience withdrawal-like symptoms while trying to abstain from pornography for a 7-day period

numbers.origin: 07-mirror-stats/porn.json hero (06-template.json hero '7 days'); quote re-fetched from the full text on 2026-11-05

problems: Severity 'heavy' does not match who was counted. The card would show 'heavy users, not checked for addiction', but they were checked. The PPCS was given, and 84.7% scored below the clinical cutoff of 76. Most were not heavy users: 61.4% used 3 or 4 times a week and 19.3% daily. The authors call it a 'non-clinical sample' and speak of 'the average regular pornography user'. That is the 'users' tag (ordinary users, not addicts). Note: kind after-first-month allows only dependent, treatment, heavy and disorder. With the correct tag, the build will refuse this number in that kind, so it needs another kind or must be held back. Holding it back is the writer's or owner's call, not a silent drop.

The headline reads as being about the reader (a hooked man, rule 2) once it sits under the mirror 'You fear the first week off will be unbearable.' The one subgroup like him, high problem scores plus daily use, felt more craving when abstaining (exploratory). The headline should name that most were not hooked.
Caveat can add from the source: 89.8% had no wish to quit. The 'high problem' level in the extra check (+1 SD, M = 72.82) was still below the clinical cutoff.

Holds: the quote is word for word (16 words). n = 176 (86 abstain, 90 control) holds, as do 64.2% female, Mage 21.38, psychology undergraduates in Malaysia, and Arch Sex Behav 52:1819-1840 (2023). The measures were taken each night for 7 days and controlled for baseline. There were 'no significant main effects of group' on craving, positive and negative affect, or withdrawal. 45.4% of the abstinence group used porn anyway. The headline is 22 words with 1 figure.
check1.applied: Applied on 2026-11-05: the reviewer's corrections word for word.
applierNotes: Build conflict, no kind change: kinds.json lets after-first-month carry dependent, treatment, heavy or disorder, not users, so build_v3.py will refuse this card under rule 3 until it moves kind or is held back. The reviewer names that as the writer's or owner's call; the applier changed neither. The only kind that takes a users number is after-body (not picked, and about body and sex rather than the first week).

Spot check, PMC9847461 full text re-fetched 2026-11-05: 'had no intrinsic desire to quit their pornography use [89.8%]' and 'high PPU at + 1 SD (i.e., M = 72.82) in this sample did not reach the clinical cutoff of ≥ 76' hold.

numbers.headline: Of 42 men on a quit-porn forum who began with erection trouble, 21 wrote that it got at least somewhat better.
numbers.mirror: You hope quitting porn will fix your erections.
numbers.counted: men on a quit-porn forum who had erection trouble

basis.design: study of online quitting journals, with no comparison group
basis.who: men aged 18 to 63 keeping a journal of a quit-porn attempt on the Reboot Nation forum
basis.n: 42 men who wrote about erection trouble at the start (of 104 journals)
basis.measured: What the men wrote about their erections during attempts lasting 7 days to 12 months.

numbers.caveat: Their own words, not a doctor's check, and nobody was compared with men who kept watching. The authors say men it helped were likelier to keep posting, and most were also stopping masturbation, so the change may not come from quitting porn alone. At most 32 of the 42 called themselves addicted. Research linking porn to erection problems is inconclusive.
numbers.weak: A forum sample of 42 men describing themselves, with no comparison group.

ref.cite: Fernandez DP, Kuss DJ, Griffiths MD (2021). The pornography “rebooting” experience: a qualitative analysis of abstinence journals on an online pornography abstinence forum. Archives of Sexual Behavior 50:711-728.
ref.quote: Of the 42 members who reported erectile difficulties at the outset of the abstinence attempt, half (n = 21) reported at least some improvements in erectile function

problems: Figure, n, quote, where, when and design hold: 'Of the 42 members who reported erectile difficulties at the outset of the abstinence attempt, half (n = 21) reported at least some improvements in erectile function' (27 words, word for word). Ages 18-63, journals 2016-2018, attempts 7 days to 12 months, Reboot Nation.

Group: the 'self-hooked' tag overstates. Table 1: 49 men reported a sexual difficulty (42 of them erectile), and only 32 reported both addiction and a sexual difficulty, so at most 32 of the 42 called themselves addicted. The card should say so.

Caveat leaves out two limits the authors state that make 21 of 42 possibly too hopeful: the sample 'likely overrepresents members who found abstinence ... beneficial' (men it did not help may just have stopped posting), and reduced masturbation 'could have contributed to improvements in sexual functioning' (86.5% of the 104 were also trying to stop masturbating).
Minor: the paper says associations between porn and sexual problems are 'generally inconclusive'; the caveat's 'whether porn causes erection problems' is a small stretch, reworded below.
Rules otherwise hold: headline 21 words, 2 figures; mirror 8 words, second person, not a screening line; no other addiction, no cheering, not a projection.
check1.applied: Applied on 2026-11-05: the reviewer's corrections word for word.
applierNotes: Spot check, PMC7889567 full text re-fetched 2026-11-05: 'the sample overrepresents members who found abstinence ... to be beneficial', 'reduction in masturbation frequency ... could have contributed to improvements in sexual functioning' and 'generally inconclusive' hold.

Build conflict from the writer's draft, not from this fix: kinds.json lets after-body carry dependent, treatment, heavy or users, not self-hooked, so build_v3.py refuses this card under rule 3. after-body is not a picked kind. The reviewer kept self-hooked (at most 32 of the 42 called themselves addicted); the applier changed neither tag nor kind.

gaps.searched: Europe PMC on 2026-11-05: porn or compulsive sexual behaviour with remission, lifetime, natural course, natural recovery and longitudinal; the 2026 expert review of the field (PMC13132360) and the 2026 three-year Budapest study's review of 12 course studies (PMC13371728).
gaps.why: No study projects the lifetime chance of getting free from a porn problem. The national surveys that give these projections for drugs never asked about porn, and the 2026 expert review says data on onset and remission are lacking. The old hero ('7 days', 06-template.json) is not a projection; it is kept under after-first-month.
gaps.fillLater: Needs a national survey; the forum harvest cannot give a lifetime share.

gaps.searched: Europe PMC on 2026-11-05 (as above, plus age with remission or recovery); Kraus 2016 (PMC5387768), Fernandez 2021 (PMC7889567) and Konkolÿ Thege 2015 (PMC4320621) full texts.
gaps.why: No porn study reports the age at which the problem ended. Kraus 2016 gives an average age of 33 for men who wanted help, which is when they were struggling, not when it ended.
gaps.fillLater: Our forum harvest could fill it: success posts that give the writer's age and how long he has been off porn.

gaps.searched: Europe PMC on 2026-11-05; Bőthe 2024 International Sex Survey (in 07); Konkolÿ Thege, Woodin, Hodgins & Williams 2015, Natural course of behavioral addictions: a 5-year longitudinal study, BMC Psychiatry 15:4 (PMC4320621, full text fetched).
gaps.why: No study counts how the people who got free did it. The nearest numbers count help-seeking among people with a problem at the time: about 1 in 10 of people at risk had ever sought treatment (Bőthe 2024, in 07), and in an Ontario cohort of people who said 'sex or pornography' caused them significant problems, 11.4% on average sought any help in a given year while most problems faded within five years (Konkolÿ Thege 2015, Table 6). Using either here would stretch it.
gaps.fillLater: Our forum harvest could fill it: success posts that name what the man used (nothing, a blocker, a group, a therapist).

gaps.searched: Europe PMC on 2026-11-05; Fernandez 2021 and Dwulit 2019 full texts.
gaps.why: The number given (4 in 10) counts past tries by men still wanting help. No porn study counts how many tries it took men who got free.
gaps.fillLater: Our forum harvest could fill it: success posts that say how many earlier attempts failed.

gaps.why: The number given (55 of 104) says how many slipped, not when. The only timed figure (45% within 7 days, in 07) counts students who were mostly not hooked and did not choose to quit.
gaps.fillLater: The felt-difficulty forum harvest could show on which days slips cluster.

gaps.searched: Europe PMC on 2026-11-05: pornography with controlled use, moderation, reduction goal or harm reduction, and abstinence; the 07 PubMed search.
gaps.why: No study compares quitting completely with cutting down for porn. Men on a quit-porn forum saw moderation as unworkable (Fernandez 2021), but that is their opinion, not a number.
gaps.fillLater: The forum harvest could count posts about each goal and what followed, but that would stay weak.

gaps.searched: Europe PMC on 2026-11-05: naltrexone, paroxetine, citalopram, escitalopram or SSRI with pornography, compulsive sexual or hypersexual, and randomized or placebo; the 2026 review of medicines for online behavioural addictions (PMID 42257421).
gaps.why: No medicine trial for porn gives a figure that reads as '1 in N'. The only placebo-controlled trial found (Wainberg 2006, PMID 17194276, abstract fetched) had 28 gay and bisexual men with compulsive sexual behaviour; citalopram reduced porn use more than placebo, with no size given. A 2026 Swedish trial (Savard, PMID 42838712, abstract fetched) compared fluoxetine with naltrexone in 80 people with the disorder, without placebo, and found no difference. The 410-man placebo trial (PMID 42919590) is a protocol with no results yet.
gaps.fillLater: Wait for the escitalopram and naltrexone placebo trial's results.

gaps.searched: Europe PMC on 2026-11-05; the 07 search (Engelhardt 2025, PMID 40483829); López-Pinar 2025 meta-analysis (PMC12231474).
gaps.why: No study measured mood after hooked men quit porn. The one-week trial found mood no worse than in those who kept watching (used under after-first-month). The 2025 meta-analysis found depression symptoms fell moderately during therapy, but that is an effect size from therapy, not a plain figure about quitting.
gaps.fillLater: Our forum harvest could fill it: posts that give a day count and describe mood.

notUsed.reason: A share of all US men who feel addicted: a screening-style number about ordinary users (rules 1 and 2), not about getting free.
Warning signs among ordinary monthly users: a screening number (rule 1).
How common daily use is: about ordinary users, and no kind in the menu covers it.
How common any use is: ordinary users, and no kind in the menu covers it (it stays in the 06 belief proof).
How common monthly use is: ordinary users, and no kind in the menu covers it.
Age at first sight of porn: about how use starts, not how it ends; no kind in the menu covers it.
Low mood and anxiety predicting daily use: about how use starts; no kind covers it.
Drift to new genres among ordinary student users: no kind in the menu covers it.
A cost of use in ordinary young men; the menu has no cost kind, and it is not about life after quitting.
Divorce link in ordinary married users; no kind in the menu covers it.

How-slips takes the forum '55 of 104', whose men mostly called themselves addicted; this trial's students were mostly not hooked and did not choose to quit. Its 45% stays in the after-first-month caveat.
Tries by ordinary student users who still watch; how-tries takes the '4 in 10' from men who wanted help.
Same ACT trial as the helps-talk card (one number per kind); its 35% stopped-completely figure is in that card's caveat.
Counts everyone who ever watched, not people who were hooked, so it cannot carry a hope kind (rule 3: no 'users' number in hope).
Shows that scores move in ordinary young adults, not a count of people who got free; hope-free-now uses a head count instead.
Help-seeking among people at risk now, not how the people who got free did it; named as the nearest number in the how-alone gap.
App installs, not people, and says nothing about quitting; 'million' is also banned in reader text (rule 11).
A count of trials, not a result a reader can picture; helps-talk takes a trial result (93% vs 21%) instead. Kept as context for the reviewers: every study in that meta-analysis was at risk of bias.
A remembered rating of unknown kinds of help: weaker than a trial result for helps-talk.
